old_entry.title: Blaster Master
old_entry.subtitle: Blaster Master Changes Perspective to Change How Space Is Understood
old_entry.summary: On June 17, 1988 Sunsoft released Chou-Wakusei Senki MetaFight in Japan, the basis for the Western version Blaster Master.
body: On June 17, 1988 Sunsoft released Chou-Wakusei Senki MetaFight in Japan, the basis for the Western version Blaster Master. The game alternates side-view exploration in the SOPHIA vehicle with top-down sections when the pilot dismounts. The shift in perspective is not decorative: it divides movement, combat and access into two grammars that feed each other, anticipating interest in interconnected worlds and abilities that open routes.

Blaster Master has two modes of gameplay that depend on the situation and location of the player: the first mode is where the player controls Jason; either on foot or piloting a tank named SOPHIA in a two–dimensional platform mode; the second mode is where the player controls Jason on foot in a top-down perspective. Gameplay in the top-down perspective consists of a series of labyrinths in which players navigate and defeat enemies along the way. Gameplay is non-linear, and players must return to earlier levels in order to advance to later levels in the game. The objective is to complete all eight levels and destroy the mutants and their bosses with various weaponry such as guns, grenades, and special weapons.

While Jason is inside SOPHIA in the 2D platforming mode, the player can attack the mutants with the main cannon (which can shoot up, left, and right determined by the orientation of the tank) or with one of three special weapons. Special weapons have limited ammunition which must be collected from exploring the game. They include the following: homing missiles that, when fired, shoot 1 missile at each enemy on screen up to 4; "Thunder Break", which fires a high-damage lightning bolt downward; and "Multi Warhead Missiles", which simultaneously fires a set of three missiles at enemies in front of and diagonally up and down. Players select their special weapon and monitor the amounts of each special weapon left by accessing the Menu Screen by pressing the Start button.

The player switches between the 2D platforming mode and the top-down perspective by leaving the tank and entering small doorways located throughout the game. While in the top-down perspective, players can move Jason in any direction and destroy mutants with a gun or with hand grenades. In this mode, players upgrade the gun by collecting gun capsules, but the gun degrades by one point if Jason receives damage from mutants or hazardous objects. Here players obtain additional vehicle functions by destroying bosses; these functions include weapon upgrades as well as abilities to swim freely underwater, drive on walls and ceilings, and hover above the ground.

The game has a glitch – colloquially known as the "grenade glitch" – to easily defeat four of the game's underbosses. old_entry.title: Super Mario Bros. 3
old_entry.subtitle: The Mushroom Kingdom Learns to Travel
old_entry.summary: World maps, transformations and secret routes expand Mario’s platforming adventure.
body: Nintendo radically expands the grammar of the first Super Mario games by introducing world maps, alternate routes, an item inventory, and transformations such as Raccoon Mario, Frog Mario, and Tanooki Mario. The ability to fly grows from a documented design compromise: flight had to be free enough to feel like a new conquest, but limited enough not to make levels built on the ground irrelevant. The game thus alternates surprise and control, turning each world into a small repertoire of rules, themes, and variations that would influence Nintendo platformers for years.

The map makes the relationship between levels visible and allows some routes to be chosen. Houses, fortresses, and moving encounters add elements that do not simply coincide with entering a new challenge. The player begins to think about the journey beyond the next jump. A stored item can be reserved for a future difficulty; an alternate road can change the order of exploration. This structure gives continuity to short episodes without turning them into one undifferentiated space. Each level retains its own form while the map organizes its relationship with the others. Progress becomes something we can observe and plan, not merely a sequence the game automatically hands us after reaching a flag.

The ability to fly as Raccoon Mario grew from a concrete level-design problem. In a Nintendo interview, Toshihiko Nakago recalled that an early version allowed flight to continue for too long, making much of the route built on the ground unnecessary. The solution was to connect takeoff to a running phase and a power meter: the player has to earn enough space before leaving the ground. Flight remains spectacular, but it does not become a switch capable of ignoring every obstacle. This compromise illustrates the method of Super Mario Bros. 3 particularly well. A new ability is evaluated not only by how fun it is on its own, but by how it changes the value of rules and spaces that already exist.

Super Mario Bros. 3 multiplies transformations and gives each one a different way of reading the level. The Super Leaf introduces a tail and flight, the Frog Suit changes control in water, the Tanooki Suit adds the statue transformation, and the Hammer Suit changes the type of attack. The manual does not present them as simple visual variations: every form has specific controls and advantages. This makes the power-up a behavioral choice, not merely a reserve of resistance to mistakes. Some areas become easier, others reveal secrets or require established habits to be adapted. The variety of transformations expands the platformer's vocabulary because it continually shifts the relationship between the character's body, terrain, and risk.

The eight kingdoms do not function only as containers for levels. Each proposes a visual or spatial rule strong enough to change what the player expects. Giant Land alters the scale of objects, Water Land shifts the emphasis to water, Sky Land builds a vertical progression, and Dark Land concentrates fortresses and dangers. The game uses this variety to prevent increasing difficulty from meaning only denser obstacles. Instead, it changes the kind of attention required. A familiar platform can become enormous, a linear route can open upward, and an aquatic environment can transform the management of inertia. The world's theme therefore guides level design and memory, allowing the player to distinguish problems even before remembering every individual stage.

Items obtained in Toad Houses and minigames can be stored and used from the map before entering a level. This possibility changes the meaning of a reward. A power-up does not have to be consumed immediately: it can become a resource reserved for an obstacle the player has not yet faced. The map thus gains a light strategic dimension. The player decides when to use a Super Star, a cloud, or a suit, and that choice can alter the risk of a route. The system remains simple to read, but introduces a memory between levels that was much more limited in the first Super Mario games. Progress is not only about what we have overcome, but also what we have chosen to save for later.

Hidden whistles, invisible blocks, areas above the screen, and optional routes make knowledge a resource that can be carried between playthroughs. Nintendo manuals and guides note that some tools can even skip entire worlds. This possibility changes the value of a secret: it is not merely a prize to collect, but a way to reorganize the journey. An experienced player can build a route different from that of someone encountering the game for the first time. Replaying does not only improve jumping precision, but changes the structure of the adventure through remembered information. Super Mario Bros. 3 thus makes curiosity part of mastery, rewarding those who try to explore edges, ceilings, and behaviors that the main route does not require.

old_entry.title: Mega Man 2
old_entry.subtitle: Every opponent leaves behind a possibility
old_entry.summary: On December 24, 1988, Capcom released Rockman 2 in Japan, later known as Mega Man 2, for Famicom.
body: On December 24, 1988, Capcom released Rockman 2 in Japan, later known as Mega Man 2, for Famicom. The sequel expands the first game's formula by increasing the selectable Robot Masters to eight and turning the choice of order into a richer network of weaknesses, weapons and routes. Capcom also introduces Energy Tanks, which allow the player to restore energy when they choose to use them, and a password system to preserve progress between sessions. The structure remains demanding, but offers more tools for planning. Levels build identity through highly specific rules, from Quick Man's intermittent darkness to Wily's platforms and hazards. Music also takes on a decisive role in the game's memory. Mega Man 2 thus refines an already recognizable grammar without making it simpler: it makes the possibilities easier to read.

Mega Man 2 increases the number of Robot Masters faced in the main part of the game to eight and preserves the freedom to choose which level to start with. Every victory grants a weapon, and that weapon can become particularly effective against another boss. The stage-select screen is therefore a small strategic problem before the platforming even begins. There is no single mandatory route, but every choice changes the tools available in later areas. The player can discover the network of weaknesses through trial and error, thematic clues or memory from previous playthroughs. This structure makes knowledge a form of power: the same level can feel very different when approached with a suitable weapon or only the Mega Buster. The sequel thus expands one of the first game's strongest ideas without changing its basic readability.

Capcom identifies Energy Tanks as one of the additions that improve quality of life over the first Mega Man. The difference is subtle but important: collected energy does not have to be consumed immediately. The player can store it and decide when to turn it into health, carrying a resource from one point in a level to a boss or later section. This possibility introduces a form of risk management that was previously much more limited. Using an E-Tank to survive a difficult encounter increases the chance of success, but means it will no longer be available for what comes next. The system does not automatically make the game easy, because the supply is finite and the platforming remains demanding. It does, however, provide a margin for personal planning, allowing players with different skill levels to build a small reserve against mistakes.

Mega Man 2 introduces a password system that preserves an essential part of progress without internal memory in the cartridge. Capcom remembers it alongside Energy Tanks as one of the sequel's improvements. The grid of dots encodes which Robot Masters have already been defeated and allows a session to be interrupted and resumed later. It is a simple technical solution that changes the relationship with difficulty. The player no longer has to complete the entire campaign in one sitting and can treat every boss as a persistent milestone. The password also becomes an object outside the game: it has to be copied down, kept and perhaps exchanged with a friend. A hardware limitation thus generates a small paper ritual. Before automatic saving, remembering an adventure literally means transcribing a code and trusting that every dot has been marked in the correct position.

The weapon system works when it forces the player to reconsider a power beyond its immediate damage. Capcom has recalled, when discussing Bubble Man, how the Bubble Lead can seem of little use in early experiments and yet gain value for revealing certain traps and, above all, at a decisive moment in the final section. This reversal makes experimentation important: a weapon should not be judged only by the first enemy it is used against. Every power has a particular trajectory, cost and function, and some become tools for exploration or situational solutions. Mega Man 2 thus strengthens the idea that defeating a boss means expanding the player's vocabulary. The reward is not a generic increase in power, but a new rule to understand, remember and connect to problems that may appear much later.

Naoya Tomita, a designer on the early Mega Man games, recalled that some of Mega Man 2's solutions arise directly from graphical limits. Discussing the Mecha Dragon battle, Capcom highlighted work on platforms created with a single color yet arranged to suggest depth, texture and shadow. It is a useful example because it shows how strongly pixel art of the period depends on economy and selection. A level cannot afford arbitrary detail, so every contrast has to help separate the character, hazards and walkable surfaces. Even a giant boss has to coexist with the space needed for jumping and reading projectiles. Restriction does not automatically guarantee good design, but it forces clear decisions. Mega Man 2 often turns those decisions into an immediately recognizable style, where color and silhouette communicate function before decoration.

Mega Man 2 ties every Robot Master to a level with a recognizable rhythm, color and musical theme, and the soundtrack has become one of the main vehicles of the game's memory. Capcom credits Takashi Tateishi with the famous theme for the first section of Wily's castle, but the effect does not depend on a single piece. The melodies have to coexist with constant sound effects, limited Famicom hardware and sessions in which the same section is repeated many times after a mistake. To work, they need to be concise, readable and capable of sustaining concentration without losing identity. Repetition, inevitable in a difficult platformer, turns the theme into an emotional map of the level. The player can remember Air Man, Bubble Man or Wily through a musical sequence as well, because sound and rule are learned at the same time.

story_headings: Every opponent leaves behind a possibility
Eight Robot Masters turn order into strategy
The Energy Tank separates recovery from the moment it is found
The password turns a series of levels into a resumable campaign
An apparently weak weapon can become the only answer
Graphical limits become a choice of form
Music gives every level an identity before the boss
